MCR-001.e: GDP is territorial and counts only final output to avoid double counting.
o: The market value of final goods and services produced within the country in a period
Total revenue of all domestic firms
Income of citizens at home and abroad
Total value of intermediate and final goods
MCR-001.x:
Basis: System of National Accounts SNA 2008 (UN, IMF, OECD, WB).
Analysis: GDP = market value of final goods and services produced within a country's territory in a period. Two keys: (1) territorial – including FDI firms operating domestically; (2) final output only (or total value added) to avoid double counting (MCR-009).
Distractors: B – total turnover double-counts intermediates; C is GNI (by residents, MCR-006); D double-counts intermediates.

MCR-002.q: Household consumption 600, investment 200, government spending 150, exports 300, imports 280 (VND trillion). What is GDP by the expenditure approach?
MCR-002.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 – expenditure approach.
Working: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) = 600 + 200 + 150 + (300 − 280) = 950 + 20 = 970 trillion VND.
Analysis: Net exports add only 20 despite large exports (300), because imports already sit in C, I and G and must be removed to count domestic output only. For Vietnam – very open to trade – net exports are small relative to gross trade.
Check: 600 + 200 + 150 + 300 − 280 = 970 ✓.

MCR-003.q: Which transaction is NOT counted in this year's GDP?
MCR-003.e: Used goods were counted when produced; only this year's brokerage service counts.
o: A household buying a 5-year-old used car (except the dealer's fee)
A firm buying new machinery produced this year
An increase in a factory's inventories
MCR-003.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (second-hand goods, distribution services).
Analysis: A used car made 5 years ago was counted in GDP in its production year; reselling it merely transfers an existing asset and creates no new output → excluded (only the brokerage fee – a service produced this year – counts).
Distractors: B – new machinery is investment I; C – teacher salaries are government spending G (buying education services); D – inventory build-up is inventory investment (MCR-014).

MCR-004.q: Nominal GDP is 1,200 and the GDP deflator is 120 (base year = 100). What is real GDP?
MCR-004.x:
Basis: SNA 2008; macroeconomics (GDP deflator).
Working: Real GDP = nominal GDP / deflator × 100 = 1,200 / 120 × 100 = 1,000 trillion VND.
Analysis: A deflator of 120 means prices are 20% above the base year; removing price effects measures real output. Note for reading data: Vietnam's statistics office reports GDP growth at constant (real) prices.
Check: 1,000 × 1.2 = 1,200 ✓.

MCR-005.q: Real GDP rises from 1,000 to 1,060. What is the growth rate (%)?
MCR-005.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (real GDP growth).
Working: Growth = (1,060 − 1,000) / 1,000 = 60 / 1,000 = 6%.
Analysis: Economic growth is measured with real GDP (constant prices), not nominal, to strip out inflation (MCR-012).

MCR-006.q: Gross national income (GNI) equals GDP plus net primary income from abroad.
MCR-006.e: True. In FDI-heavy economies repatriating profits, GNI is usually below GDP.
MCR-006.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (GNI = GDP + net primary income from abroad).
Analysis: True. GNI measures residents' income; primary income covers cross-border wages, profits, interest and dividends. Economies with heavy FDI profit repatriation (like Vietnam) have negative net primary income → GNI < GDP (MCR-007).
Note: Remittances are secondary income, counted not in GNI but in gross national disposable income (GNDI).

MCR-007.q: GDP is USD 500 billion; net primary income from abroad is −20 billion (large FDI profit outflows). What is GNI (USD billion)?
MCR-007.x:
Basis: SNA 2008.
Working: GNI = GDP + net primary income = 500 + (−20) = USD 480 billion.
Analysis: GNI/GDP = 96% → 4% of value created on the territory accrues to foreign investors. For living standards, GNI per capita (which the World Bank uses for income groups) is a closer gauge than GDP.
Check: 480 / 500 = 96% ✓.

MCR-008.q: Match each GDP approach with its calculation:
MCR-008.e: In theory the three give the same result; statistical discrepancies are shown separately.
p: Sum of value added + product taxes less subsidies
Compensation of employees + operating surplus + depreciation + net production taxes
MCR-008.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (three GDP approaches).
Analysis: Production – total value added by industry (output − intermediate consumption) + product taxes − product subsidies. Expenditure – C + I + G + (X − M). Income – compensation of employees + operating surplus + consumption of fixed capital + net production taxes. In theory all three agree; in practice a statistical discrepancy arises from different data sources.

MCR-009.q: A farmer sells rice to a mill for 100; the mill sells flour to a bakery for 160; the bakery sells bread to consumers for 250 (no other inputs). What is the contribution to GDP?
MCR-009.e: Total value added = 100 + 60 + 90 = 250 = value of the final product.
MCR-009.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (value added).
Working: Value added: farmer 100 − 0 = 100; mill 160 − 100 = 60; bakery 250 − 160 = 90; total = 100 + 60 + 90 = 250 = value of the final product (bread).
Analysis: Summing sales at each stage (100 + 160 + 250 = 510) double-counts intermediates. That's why GDP counts only final output or total value added (MCR-001).

MCR-010.q: Transfer payments (pensions, unemployment benefits) are counted in government spending G in GDP.
MCR-010.e: False. Transfers aren't payments for newly produced goods or services, so they're not in G.
MCR-010.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (government final consumption, transfers).
Analysis: False. G covers only purchases of goods and services (civil servant pay, procurement, public investment). Pensions and unemployment benefits are transfers – not exchanged for newly produced output → not in G. They affect GDP only indirectly when recipients spend (via C).

MCR-011.q: The key difference between the GDP deflator and the CPI:
MCR-011.e: So imported fuel price rises affect the CPI more than the GDP deflator.
o: The deflator covers all domestically produced goods with changing weights; the CPI uses a fixed consumer basket including imports
MCR-011.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; the statistics office's CPI methodology.
Analysis: The GDP deflator covers all domestically produced goods and services (including investment and exports), with weights shifting with output each year. The CPI uses a fixed consumer basket (weights updated periodically), including imports but excluding investment goods. Hence imported fuel price rises hit the CPI harder than the deflator.
Distractors: B – the CPI excludes investment machinery; C is wrong; D – the two usually differ.

MCR-012.q: Year 1: nominal GDP 800, deflator 100. Year 2: nominal GDP 920, deflator 110. What is real GDP growth in year 2 (%, 2 decimals)?
MCR-012.e: Real GDP year 2 = 920/1.1 ≈ 836.36; growth = 836.36/800 − 1 ≈ 4.55%. Most of the 15% nominal growth is price.
MCR-012.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics.
Working: Real GDP year 1 = 800 / 1.00 = 800; year 2 = 920 / 1.10 ≈ 836.36; real growth = 836.36 / 800 − 1 ≈ 4.55%.
Analysis: Nominal growth = 920 / 800 − 1 = 15%, of which prices rose 10% → (1.15 / 1.10) − 1 ≈ 4.55% is real. For company analysis: high nominal revenue growth amid inflation isn't necessarily real growth.
Check: 1.0455 × 1.10 ≈ 1.15 ✓.

MCR-013.q: Select ALL limitations of GDP as a welfare measure:
MCR-013.e: The informal sector is often underestimated or hard to measure.
o: Fully and accurately covers the informal sector
MCR-013.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Report (2009) on measuring economic performance and social progress.
Analysis: GDP's limits: (A) it omits non-market household production (housework, care); (B) it doesn't deduct environmental degradation or resource depletion; (C) it ignores income distribution (averages hide inequality); (D) it doesn't value leisure.
Distractors: (E) The informal sector is usually underestimated and hard to measure.

MCR-014.q: An increase in business inventories is counted as investment (I) in GDP.
MCR-014.e: True. Output produced but unsold is counted as inventory investment.
MCR-014.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (capital formation – changes in inventories).
Analysis: True. Goods produced but unsold in the period count as investment (inventory change) so GDP reflects production regardless of sale. When sold later, inventories fall (negative inventory investment), offsetting higher consumption.
Note: Unintended inventory build-up (unsold goods) is often an early sign of weakening demand.

MCR-015.q: GDP is USD 480 billion, population 100 million. What is GDP per capita (USD)?
MCR-015.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics.
Working: GDP per capita = USD 480 billion / 100 million people = 480 × 10⁹ / 100 × 10⁶ = USD 4,800 per person.
Analysis: Per-capita figures compare living standards; supplement them with PPP measures and GNI per capita to adjust for price levels and income sent abroad (MCR-007).

MCR-016.q: The CPI was 150 last year and 156 this year. What is the inflation rate (%)?
MCR-016.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (CPI inflation).
Working: Inflation = (156 − 150) / 150 = 6 / 150 = 4%.
Analysis: Inflation is the growth rate of the price index, not its level. Distinguish reporting bases: year-on-year, annual average versus prior year, and versus December of the prior year (YTD) – the statistics office publishes all three.

MCR-017.q: The nominal deposit rate is 7% and expected inflation 4%. What is the approximate real rate (simple Fisher) (%)?
MCR-017.x:
Basis: Fisher equation (1930): (1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + πᵉ).
Working: Approximation: r ≈ i − πᵉ = 7% − 4% = 3%. Exact: r = 1.07 / 1.04 − 1 ≈ 2.88%.
Analysis: The real rate drives saving and investment decisions. For investors: comparing expected equity returns (or earnings yield E/P) with real rates helps gauge the opportunity cost of capital.

MCR-018.q: The labour force is 50 million, unemployed 1.1 million. What is the unemployment rate (%)?
MCR-018.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; ILO definition (unemployed: without work, seeking work, available).
Working: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force = 1.1 / 50 = 2.2%.
Analysis: The denominator is the labour force (employed + unemployed), not population. Vietnam's low rate partly reflects large informal and farm sectors – look also at underemployment.
Check: 50 × 2.2% = 1.1 ✓.

MCR-019.q: Match each type of unemployment with an example:
MCR-019.e: Natural unemployment comprises frictional and structural; cyclical unemployment tracks recessions.
p: A new engineering graduate searching for a suitable job
A handloom weaver displaced by automation, lacking new skills
Construction workers laid off in a recession
Tour guides out of work in the low season
MCR-019.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (types of unemployment).
Analysis: Frictional – time spent finding a suitable job (a new graduate engineer). Structural – skill/sector mismatch from technological or structural change (handloom weavers displaced by automation). Cyclical – from falling aggregate demand in recessions (construction workers). Seasonal – by season (tour guides off-peak).
Note: Natural unemployment = frictional + structural (MCR-020).

MCR-020.q: The natural rate of unemployment comprises:
MCR-020.e: At potential output, cyclical unemployment is zero.
MCR-020.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (Friedman 1968 – natural rate of unemployment).
Analysis: The natural rate = frictional + structural unemployment – present even at potential output, where cyclical unemployment is zero. Demand policy can only cut cyclical unemployment; lowering the natural rate needs structural policy (training, job-matching).
Distractors: B, C and D misdefine it.

MCR-021.q: The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment; in the long run it is vertical at the natural rate.
MCR-021.e: True. Once expectations adjust, higher inflation can't keep unemployment below the natural rate permanently.
MCR-021.x:
Basis: Phillips (1958); Friedman (1968), Phelps (1967) – expectations-augmented Phillips curve.
Analysis: True. Short run: unexpectedly high inflation cuts real wages, firms hire more → unemployment falls (inverse relation). Long run: expectations adjust, nominal wages catch up → unemployment returns to the natural rate at higher inflation → a vertical long-run curve. Implication: inflation can't hold unemployment below the natural rate permanently.

MCR-022.q: A classic example of cost-push inflation is:
MCR-022.e: The other options are demand-pull sources.
o: A sharp rise in world oil prices raising transport and production costs
MCR-022.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (cost-push vs demand-pull inflation).
Analysis: Cost-push: rising production costs shift SRAS left (MCR-064) – a sharp oil price rise lifts transport and production costs → higher prices, lower output.
Distractors: B, C and D – credit booms, more public investment and an export boom raise aggregate demand → demand-pull inflation (MCR-075).
Note: In Vietnam, fuel, food and administered electricity prices are common cost-push sources.

MCR-023.q: Select ALL groups usually hurt by unexpectedly high inflation:
MCR-023.e: Fixed-rate borrowers gain because the real value of debt falls.
o: Workers on fixed nominal long-term wages
MCR-023.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (redistributive effects of unexpected inflation).
Analysis: Higher-than-expected inflation shifts wealth: (A) fixed-rate lenders lose – repaid in cheaper money; (B) cash holders lose purchasing power; (C) long-term fixed nominal wages → falling real pay; (D) pensions not indexed promptly.
Distractors: (E) Fixed-rate borrowers gain as the real debt shrinks.
Note: For investing – firms with fixed-rate debt and real assets (property, inventories) often benefit from surprise inflation.

MCR-024.q: Under Okun's law (each 1 point of unemployment above the natural rate puts output 2% below potential), actual unemployment is 6% and the natural rate 4.5%. What is the output gap (%)?
MCR-024.x:
Basis: Okun's law (1962).
Working: Output gap ≈ −2 × (u − u*) = −2 × (6 − 4.5) = −2 × 1.5 = −3%.
Analysis: Output is 3% below potential. The Okun coefficient (2 here) is empirical and varies across countries and periods; with large informal sectors the relation is usually weaker.

MCR-025.q: Deflation (a sustained fall in prices) is always good because people buy cheaper.
MCR-025.e: False. Persistent deflation raises real debt burdens, delays spending and cuts investment.
MCR-025.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Fisher (1933) – debt deflation.
Analysis: False. Prolonged deflation: raises the real debt burden (real debt grows as nominal income falls) → defaults; consumers delay purchases awaiting lower prices; firms cut investment while nominal wages resist cuts → unemployment; real rates rise once nominal rates hit zero (MCR-039). Example: Japan, 1990s–2010s.
Note: Productivity-driven price falls ('good' deflation) differ from demand-driven deflation.

MCR-026.e: Usually caused by adverse supply shocks; policy faces conflicting goals.
o: High inflation with low growth and high unemployment
MCR-026.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (1970s oil shocks).
Analysis: Stagflation = high inflation + low/negative growth + high unemployment, usually from an adverse supply shock (SRAS shifts left – MCR-064). Policy is hard because goals conflict: stimulus raises inflation, tightening deepens recession (MCR-070).
Note: For portfolios, stagflation tends to hurt both equities and bonds; commodities and real assets may fare better.

MCR-027.q: The working-age population is 70 million and the labour force 52.5 million. What is the participation rate (%)?
MCR-027.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; ILO.
Working: Participation rate = labour force / working-age population = 52.5 / 70 = 75%.
Analysis: The other 25% are outside the labour force (students, homemakers, retirees, discouraged workers – MCR-028). Falling participation can make unemployment fall 'artificially'.
Check: 70 × 75% = 52.5 ✓.

MCR-028.q: 'Discouraged workers' (who want work but stopped searching) are counted as unemployed.
MCR-028.e: False. They're outside the labour force, so the unemployment rate may understate true slack.
MCR-028.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; ILO definition (the unemployed must be seeking work).
Analysis: False. Discouraged workers want jobs but have stopped searching → they fail the 'seeking work' test → outside the labour force, not counted as unemployed. So the official rate may understate real slack; look also at underemployment and participation.

MCR-029.e: It separates underlying inflation from temporary shocks.
o: Volatile items such as fresh food, energy and administered prices
MCR-029.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; the statistics office's core inflation method.
Analysis: Core inflation excludes volatile items hit by temporary shocks: food, fresh produce and energy; in Vietnam also state-administered prices (healthcare, education). It separates underlying (demand/monetary) inflation from supply shocks – key for monetary policy.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the exclusions.

MCR-030.q: Nominal wages rise 8% and inflation is 5%. By how much do real wages rise (exact, %, 2 decimals)?
MCR-030.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (real wages – Fisher relation).
Working: Real wage growth = 1.08 / 1.05 − 1 = 1.028571 − 1 ≈ 2.86% (approximation: 8 − 5 = 3%).
Analysis: The approximation error grows with inflation. The same applies to real revenue growth of companies or a portfolio's real return.
Check: 1.0286 × 1.05 ≈ 1.08 ✓.

MCR-031.q: Match each function of money with an example:
MCR-031.e: High inflation erodes the store-of-value function first.
p: Paying for goods instead of bartering
Pricing goods and keeping accounts in dong
MCR-031.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (functions of money).
Analysis: Medium of exchange – a payment intermediary avoiding barter's 'double coincidence of wants'. Unit of account – a common measure for prices and financial statements. Store of value – carrying purchasing power into the future.
Note: High inflation erodes the store-of-value function first (people move to gold, USD, property – dollarisation), then the unit of account.

MCR-032.q: Simple money multiplier: required reserve ratio 8%, no excess reserves, no cash holding. What is the multiplier?
MCR-032.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (simple money multiplier).
Working: Money multiplier m = 1 / reserve ratio = 1 / 0.08 = 12.5×.
Analysis: Each unit of reserves (base money) can support up to 12.5 units of deposits. In practice the multiplier is smaller due to cash holding (leakage), excess reserves and limited credit demand. Extended formula: m = (1 + c) / (r + e + c), with c the currency ratio and e excess reserves.

MCR-033.q: A new deposit of VND 100 billion enters the banking system; reserve ratio 5%, no cash leakage or excess reserves. What maximum total deposits are created (VND billion)?
MCR-033.e: 100 × 1/0.05 = 2,000 billion (including the initial 100). In reality it's smaller due to leakages and excess reserves.
MCR-033.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (bank money creation).
Working: Maximum total deposits = initial deposit × 1 / reserve ratio = 100 × 1 / 0.05 = 100 × 20 = VND 2,000 billion (including the initial 100); new deposits created = 1,900 billion.
Analysis: The lend–redeposit chain: 100 + 95 + 90.25 + … = 100 / (1 − 0.95) = 2,000. Actual figures are smaller due to cash leakage and excess reserves.
Check: 2,000 × 5% = 100 in reserves ✓.

MCR-034.q: When the central bank buys securities in open market operations, it:
MCR-034.e: Selling or issuing bills does the opposite: drains liquidity.
o: Adds bank reserves, raising money supply and pushing interbank rates down
Has no effect on money supply
MCR-034.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Law on the State Bank of Vietnam 2010 Arts. 10, 15 (open market operations).
Analysis: Central bank purchases of securities (government bonds, bills) → payment into banks' reserve accounts → more reserves and system liquidity → lower interbank rates, possibly more money supply. Selling or issuing SBV bills → draining liquidity, higher rates.
Distractors: B describes selling; C – there is an effect; D – buying local-currency paper doesn't directly cut FX reserves.
Note: For investors, net OMO injections/withdrawals and interbank rates are short-term liquidity indicators.

MCR-035.q: Select ALL monetary policy instruments the State Bank of Vietnam can use:
MCR-035.e: Tax is a fiscal tool decided by the National Assembly and Government.
MCR-035.x:
Basis: Law on the State Bank of Vietnam 46/2010/QH12 Art. 10 (monetary policy instruments).
Analysis: SBV tools: (A) open market operations; (B) refinancing and rates (refinancing, rediscount); (C) reserve requirements; (D) exchange rates and FX market intervention. The SBV also uses administrative tools such as credit growth quotas (credit 'room') – specific to Vietnam.
Distractors: (E) CIT is a fiscal tool set by the National Assembly and Government.

MCR-036.q: Other things equal, a central bank raising its policy rate tends to make the domestic currency appreciate.
MCR-036.e: True. Wider rate differentials attract capital and make domestic assets more attractive.
MCR-036.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics (uncovered interest parity, capital flows).
Analysis: True. A higher policy rate widens the domestic–foreign rate gap → local assets become more attractive, capital flows in, FX speculation eases → upward pressure on the currency (or less depreciation pressure). That's why emerging-market central banks hike when the Fed tightens and the USD strengthens.
Note: Actual effects also depend on country risk, inflation expectations and capital controls.

MCR-037.q: Using MV = PY: money grows 10%, velocity is constant, real output grows 6%. What is approximate inflation (%)?
MCR-037.x:
Basis: Quantity theory of money (Fisher; Friedman) – MV = PY.
Working: Growth form: %ΔM + %ΔV ≈ %ΔP + %ΔY → %ΔP ≈ 10 + 0 − 6 = 4%.
Analysis: Money growing faster than real output shows up in prices. In practice velocity V is unstable (shifting with rates and financial innovation), so the relation mainly holds in the long run.

MCR-038.q: Which is NOT a monetary policy transmission channel?
MCR-038.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (Mishkin – monetary transmission channels).
Analysis: Transmission channels: interest rates (cost of capital → investment, consumption); credit (banks' lending capacity); exchange rates (trade); asset prices (wealth effect, Tobin's q) and expectations. An environmental protection tax is a fiscal tool → not a monetary channel.
Note: In bank-dominated Vietnam the credit channel matters most; for equities, asset-price and expectation channels act directly.

MCR-039.q: In a 'liquidity trap', with nominal rates near zero, adding money has little effect on aggregate demand.
MCR-039.e: True. People hold money rather than bonds; fiscal policy or forward guidance works better.
MCR-039.x:
Basis: Keynes (1936) – liquidity trap; Krugman (1998).
Analysis: True. With nominal rates near zero (the lower bound), people happily hold money instead of bonds yielding almost nothing → more money can't push rates lower and barely moves demand. Then fiscal policy, forward guidance and QE buying long-term assets (MCR-042) work better. Examples: Japan, the US and Europe after 2008.

MCR-040.q: The main argument for central bank independence is:
MCR-040.e: Evidence shows higher independence tends to coincide with lower inflation.
o: Credible commitment to price stability, reducing 'inflation bias' from short-term political pressure
Cheaper central bank lending to the budget
MCR-040.x:
Basis: Kydland & Prescott (1977), Barro & Gordon (1983) – inflation bias; Alesina & Summers (1993).
Analysis: An independent central bank makes price-stability commitments more credible, reducing 'inflation bias' from short-term political pressure (pre-election stimulus, money-financed deficits). Empirically, higher independence goes with lower inflation without lower growth.
Distractors: B – independence restricts lending to the budget; C and D aren't the argument.
Note: The SBV is a Government agency – less independent than many central banks.

MCR-041.q: The desired real rate is 2% and expected inflation 3.5%. What is the approximate nominal rate (%)?
MCR-041.x:
Basis: Fisher equation.
Working: i ≈ r + πᵉ = 2% + 3.5% = 5.5% (exact: 1.02 × 1.035 − 1 = 5.57%).
Analysis: Nominal rates must compensate expected inflation for savers to earn their desired real return. In valuation: a nominal cost of equity (Ke) must match nominal cash flows – never mix real cash flows with nominal discount rates.

MCR-042.e: QE expands the central bank balance sheet; unwinding it is quantitative tightening (QT).
o: Large-scale central bank asset purchases (long bonds) to lower long yields when short rates are near zero
MCR-042.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Bernanke (2020) – unconventional monetary policy.
Analysis: QE: the central bank buys large amounts of assets (long-term government bonds, MBS) with new reserves → lowering long-term yields (portfolio balance channel), lifting asset prices and signalling low rates for longer – used when short rates are near zero (MCR-039). The balance sheet expands; unwinding is QT.
Distractors: B is fiscal; C is tightening; D is FX intervention.
Note: Fed QE/QT strongly affects global liquidity and emerging-market flows.

MCR-043.q: Raising the reserve requirement increases the money multiplier.
MCR-043.e: False. The multiplier falls as banks hold more reserves and lend less.
MCR-043.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (MCR-032).
Analysis: False. m = 1 / r: a higher reserve ratio → banks hold more reserves per deposit and lend less → a smaller multiplier and money supply. E.g., r from 5% to 8%: m falls from 20 to 12.5. Raising reserve requirements is a tightening tool (MCR-044).

MCR-044.q: Select ALL signs of monetary tightening:
MCR-044.e: Cutting the refinancing rate is an easing move.
o: Net liquidity withdrawal via bill issuance
MCR-044.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; SBV Law 2010.
Analysis: Tightening signs: (A) higher policy rates; (B) net liquidity withdrawal via SBV bill issuance; (C) higher reserve requirements; (D) lower or tighter credit growth quotas.
Distractors: (E) Cutting the refinancing rate is easing.
Note (FERGASITOR application): the macro–cycle layer should track a combination of signals (interbank rates, OMO, bills, credit room, FX) rather than one; monetary tightening usually weighs on P/E valuations and rate-sensitive sectors (property, brokers).

MCR-045.e: M1 = currency + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + time and savings deposits.
o: Currency in circulation, demand deposits, and time and savings deposits
MCR-045.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; SBV monetary statistics.
Analysis: M0 – currency in circulation (plus reserves = base money); M1 = currency + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + time and savings deposits (total means of payment). In Vietnam, M2 also includes foreign-currency deposits of residents and organisations.
Distractors: B and C omit components; D – shares aren't money.
Note: M2 and credit growth are key macro liquidity indicators for Vietnam's stock market.

MCR-046.q: A bank has capital of 10, total assets of 120 and risk-weighted assets of 100 (VND trillion). What is the (simple) capital adequacy ratio (%)?
MCR-046.x:
Basis: Basel II/III (capital adequacy); Circular 41/2016/TT-NHNN (8% minimum CAR under Basel II in Vietnam).
Working: CAR = capital / risk-weighted assets = 10 / 100 = 10%.
Analysis: The denominator is RWA, not total assets (120) – using total assets gives an 8.3% leverage ratio. A 10% CAR beats the 8% minimum but with a thin buffer – constraining credit growth without new capital.
Note (bank analysis, e.g., CTG/BID/VCB): low CAR forces retained earnings, stock dividends or issuance → affecting ROE and P/B.

MCR-047.q: Under inflation targeting, the central bank announces an inflation target and adjusts the policy rate so forecast inflation converges to it.
MCR-047.e: True. Transparency and communication are key to anchoring expectations.
MCR-047.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Svensson (1997) – inflation targeting; practice at RBNZ (1990) and major central banks.
Analysis: True. Inflation targeting: announce a target (often 2% in advanced economies), forecast inflation and move the policy rate so forecast inflation converges on the target; transparency and communication (minutes, policy reports) are key to anchoring expectations.
Note: Vietnam sets an annual inflation goal in its socio-economic plan (often about 4–4.5%) but pursues multiple objectives (growth, FX), not pure inflation targeting.

MCR-048.q: Under the Taylor principle, when inflation exceeds target by 1 point, the policy rate should:
MCR-048.e: The 'Taylor principle': raise nominal rates more than inflation to genuinely tighten.
o: Rise by more than 1 point so the real rate rises
MCR-048.x:
Basis: Taylor (1993), 'Discretion versus policy rules in practice'.
Analysis: Taylor rule: i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap). With inflation 1 point above target, the nominal rate rises 1.5 points (coefficient > 1 – the Taylor principle) → the real rate rises, genuinely tightening. Raising exactly 1 point leaves the real rate unchanged; less than 1 cuts it – implicit easing.
Distractors: B, C and D are insufficient or the wrong direction.

MCR-049.q: MPC is 0.8 in a closed economy with no proportional taxes. What is the government spending multiplier?
MCR-049.x:
Basis: Keynesian model (spending multiplier).
Working: k = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / (1 − 0.8) = 1 / 0.2 = 5×.
Analysis: Government spending +1 → income +1 → consumption +0.8 → … total = 1 / (1 − 0.8) = 5. Real multipliers are far smaller due to proportional taxes (MCR-072), imports (leakage) and crowding out (MCR-052); empirical estimates are often 0.5–2.

MCR-050.q: MPC is 0.75. What is the magnitude (absolute value) of the lump-sum tax multiplier?
MCR-050.e: Tax multiplier = −MPC/(1 − MPC) = −0.75/0.25 = −3; magnitude 3, smaller than the spending multiplier (4).
MCR-050.x:
Basis: Keynesian model (tax multiplier).
Working: Tax multiplier = −MPC / (1 − MPC) = −0.75 / 0.25 = −3 → magnitude 3. Spending multiplier = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
Analysis: A tax cut of 1 raises initial consumption by only 0.75 (the rest is saved) → the tax multiplier is exactly 1 below the spending multiplier. This underpins the balanced-budget multiplier of 1 (MCR-051).

MCR-051.q: Government raises spending by 100 and lump-sum taxes by exactly 100 (balanced budget). In the simple Keynesian model, how much does GDP change?
MCR-051.e: The balanced-budget multiplier is 1 → GDP rises by 100.
MCR-051.x:
Basis: Keynesian model (Haavelmo theorem – balanced-budget multiplier).
Working: ΔY = ΔG × 1/(1 − MPC) − ΔT × MPC/(1 − MPC) = ΔG × (1 − MPC)/(1 − MPC) = ΔG × 1 = 100 (with ΔG = ΔT = 100).
Analysis: Check with MPC 0.8: spending +100 × 5 = 500; tax −100 × 4 = −400; net +100. The result doesn't depend on MPC in the simple model (lump-sum tax, closed economy).

MCR-052.q: Crowding out occurs when heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment.
MCR-052.e: True. It's larger near full employment and with limited capital mobility.
MCR-052.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (IS–LM; crowding out).
Analysis: True. Heavy government borrowing → more demand for loanable funds → higher rates → less private investment (and durable consumption), partly offsetting the stimulus. Crowding out is stronger near full employment, without central bank accommodation and with immobile capital; weaker in deep recessions with rates near zero.
Note: In Vietnam, large government bond issuance may compete for funds with banks and firms.

MCR-053.q: An example of an 'automatic stabiliser' is:
MCR-053.e: They automatically cut taxes and raise spending in recessions without new decisions.
o: Progressive income tax and unemployment benefits
A stimulus package passed by parliament
MCR-053.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (automatic stabilisers).
Analysis: Automatic stabilisers respond to the cycle with no new decisions: progressive income tax – in a downturn incomes fall and taxes fall faster; unemployment benefits – spending rises in recessions → supporting demand; the reverse in booms.
Distractors: B and D are discretionary fiscal policy (need decisions); C is monetary policy.

MCR-054.q: Public debt/GDP is 40%; the primary balance is zero; the average nominal interest rate on debt is 6%; nominal GDP growth 8%. What is next year's debt/GDP (%, 2 decimals)?
MCR-054.e: d' = d × (1 + i)/(1 + g) = 40 × 1.06/1.08 ≈ 39.26%. When g > i the ratio falls without a primary surplus.
MCR-054.x:
Basis: Public debt dynamics: d(t+1) = d(t) × (1 + i)/(1 + g) − primary balance/GDP.
Working: d' = 40% × 1.06 / 1.08 − 0 = 40% × 0.98148 ≈ 39.26%.
Analysis: When nominal growth (8%) exceeds the nominal interest rate on debt (6%), debt/GDP falls on its own even with a balanced primary budget ('i − g < 0'). If i > g, a primary surplus is needed to stabilise debt.
Check: 39.26 × 1.08 ≈ 42.4 = 40 × 1.06 ✓.

MCR-055.q: Under 'Ricardian equivalence', a debt-financed tax cut doesn't raise consumption because households save for higher future taxes.
MCR-055.e: True in theory; only partly in practice due to liquidity constraints and short horizons.
MCR-055.x:
Basis: Barro (1974), 'Are Government Bonds Net Wealth?'; Ricardo.
Analysis: True (in theory). Rational, far-sighted households with perfect capital markets see a debt-financed tax cut today as higher taxes tomorrow → they save the cut → consumption unchanged, no stimulus. In practice it holds only partly: liquidity constraints, short horizons and non-lump-sum taxes mean tax cuts still have effects.

MCR-056.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (expansionary fiscal policy).
Analysis: Fiscal expansion: (A) accelerating public investment disbursement – directly raising G; (B) tax cuts and deferrals – lifting disposable income and corporate cash flow; (C) higher social transfers; (D) lower fees and charges. Vietnam used many of these (2% VAT cut, tax and land-rent deferrals) during 2020–2025.
Distractors: (E) Raising VAT rates is tightening.

MCR-057.q: Budget revenue 1,800; total spending 2,000 including interest of 100. What is the primary balance?
MCR-057.x:
Basis: Public finance (IMF GFSM 2014 – primary balance).
Working: Primary spending = 2,000 − 100 = 1,900; primary balance = 1,800 − 1,900 = −100 trillion VND; overall balance = 1,800 − 2,000 = −200 (deficit).
Analysis: The primary balance excludes interest – showing the current fiscal stance, used in debt sustainability analysis (MCR-054).
Check: −100 − 100 interest = −200 ✓.

MCR-058.q: Compared with monetary policy, fiscal policy typically has:
MCR-058.e: Public investment in many countries, including Vietnam, often faces disbursement delays.
o: Longer decision and implementation lags (approval, disbursement) but a more direct effect on demand
MCR-058.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (policy lags: recognition, decision, implementation, impact).
Analysis: Fiscal policy has longer decision and implementation lags (parliamentary approval, investment procedures, disbursement), but once enacted acts more directly on demand (G is a GDP component). Monetary policy is decided quickly (by the central bank) but transmits indirectly with 6–18 month impact lags.
Note: Slow public investment disbursement is chronic in Vietnam – a macro variable to watch for construction and materials (steel, cement, aggregates).

MCR-059.q: The structural (cyclically adjusted) balance removes cyclical effects on revenue and spending to assess the fiscal stance.
MCR-059.e: True. A wider deficit in recession may be purely cyclical, not active easing.
MCR-059.x:
Basis: IMF (cyclically adjusted balance); macroeconomics.
Analysis: True. The structural balance = actual balance minus cyclical effects (lower revenue, higher social spending in recessions) – estimated at potential output. A deficit widening in recession may reflect only automatic stabilisers (MCR-053), not active easing; conversely, boom-time surpluses may hide structural deficits.

MCR-060.q: How does public investment in transport infrastructure affect the economy?
MCR-060.e: Project quality (selection, cost, timing) determines the long-run effect.
o: Raises demand in the short run; raises potential output in the long run if projects are efficient
MCR-060.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (Aschauer 1989 – public capital and productivity).
Analysis: Infrastructure investment: short run, it lifts aggregate demand (materials, labour – multiplier); long run, it raises potential output if projects are efficient (lower logistics costs, wider markets, higher private productivity). Effectiveness hinges on project selection, cost, timing and management; poor projects only add debt.
Distractors: B, C and D miss one dimension.

MCR-061.q: Tax revenue is VND 1,500 trillion and GDP 12,000. What is the tax-to-GDP ratio (%)?
MCR-061.x:
Basis: Public finance.
Working: Tax-to-GDP = 1,500 / 12,000 = 12.5%.
Analysis: The tax-to-GDP ratio shows revenue mobilisation capacity; international comparisons need consistent definitions (taxes only, or including fees, social contributions, land and crude-oil revenue).
Check: 12,000 × 12.5% = 1,500 ✓.

MCR-062.e: Where the peak lies is an empirical, contested question.
o: Beyond some rate, raising tax rates can reduce total revenue
MCR-062.x:
Basis: Laffer (1974); supply-side economics.
Analysis: The Laffer curve: revenue = rate × base; a 0% rate raises nothing, and a 100% rate raises almost nothing (no one works or reports). A maximum lies between; beyond it, higher rates shrink the base (less work and investment, more evasion) faster → lower revenue. Where the peak lies is empirical and contested.
Distractors: B, C and D contradict the theory.

MCR-063.q: The aggregate demand (AD) curve shifts right when:
MCR-063.e: Oil and productivity affect supply; a price-level change is a move along AD.
o: Consumer and business confidence rise sharply
The price level rises (a move along AD)
MCR-063.x:
Basis: AD–AS model.
Analysis: AD shifts right when a spending component rises at every price level: stronger consumer and business confidence (C and I up); also higher government spending, exports or money supply.
Distractors: B and C – higher oil prices and lower productivity act on supply (SRAS left); D – a price-level change is a movement along AD, not a shift.

MCR-064.q: Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) shifts left when:
MCR-064.e: Result: higher prices and lower output (adverse supply shock).
o: Input costs such as energy and materials rise
MCR-064.x:
Basis: AD–AS model.
Analysis: SRAS shifts left when production costs rise at every price level: energy, materials or nominal wages up, disasters, supply-chain disruptions. Result: higher prices, lower output – an adverse supply shock (MCR-022, MCR-026).
Distractors: B, C and D act on demand (AD shifts right).

MCR-065.q: Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) is vertical at potential output.
MCR-065.e: True. In the long run, output depends on resources and technology, not the price level.
MCR-065.x:
Basis: AD–AS model (classical long run).
Analysis: True. In the long run, prices and wages fully adjust → output is set by resources (labour, capital), technology and institutions, independent of the price level → LRAS is vertical at potential output. Demand policy then only changes prices; raising potential needs supply-side policy (MCR-095).

MCR-066.q: Arrange the business cycle phases starting from the trough:
MCR-066.e: Phase length and amplitude differ across cycles.
MCR-066.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Burns & Mitchell (1946) – business cycles.
Analysis: Cycle: trough → recovery–expansion (output up, unemployment down) → peak (output above potential, rising inflation) → contraction–recession → new trough. Phase length and amplitude vary.
Note (investing): in FERGASITOR, identifying the cycle phase is the first layer; cyclical sectors (steel, property, brokers, banks) need normalised-earnings valuation – a low P/E at peak earnings can be a value trap.

MCR-067.q: Actual real GDP is 950 and potential 1,000. What is the output gap (%)?
MCR-067.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (output gap).
Working: Output gap = (Y − Y*) / Y* = (950 − 1,000) / 1,000 = −5%.
Analysis: A negative gap → the economy is below potential with idle resources and low inflation pressure → room to ease. Potential output is unobservable and must be estimated (HP filter, production function) → sizeable uncertainty.

MCR-068.q: Select ALL indicators usually treated as LEADING cycle indicators:
MCR-068.e: Unemployment is usually a lagging indicator.
o: The slope of the yield curve
MCR-068.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; Conference Board leading indicators (LEI).
Analysis: Leading indicators move ahead of the cycle: (A) PMI and new orders – future production; (B) new building permits; (C) stock indices – expected earnings; (D) yield-curve slope (MCR-071).
Distractors: (E) Unemployment is lagging – firms are slow to lay off and slow to rehire.
Note: For Vietnam, the manufacturing PMI (S&P Global), credit growth and export orders are useful leading indicators.

MCR-069.q: In the short run, a positive demand shock raises both output and the price level.
MCR-069.e: True. AD shifts right along an upward-sloping SRAS.
MCR-069.x:
Basis: AD–AS model.
Analysis: True. A positive demand shock (AD shifts right) along an upward-sloping SRAS → both output and the price level rise in the short run. In the long run, wages and prices adjust (SRAS shifts left) → output returns to potential at a higher price level.

MCR-070.q: After an adverse supply shock, the central bank faces a hard choice because:
MCR-070.e: This is the classic trade-off with supply-driven inflation.
o: Stimulating to protect output raises inflation; tightening to curb inflation cuts output further
MCR-070.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (policy trade-off under supply shocks).
Analysis: An adverse supply shock raises prices and cuts output at once. The central bank must choose: stimulate to protect output → higher inflation, risking unanchored expectations; tighten to curb inflation → deeper output losses. It can't achieve both.
Distractors: B – tools exist; C – inflation rises, not falls; D – the shock doesn't vanish immediately.
Note: If the shock is temporary and expectations anchored, central banks often 'look through' first-round effects.

MCR-071.q: An inverted yield curve (short yields above long) is often seen as:
MCR-071.e: It reflects expected future policy rate cuts; reliability varies over time.
o: A recession warning in advanced economies
A sure sign of prolonged overheating
A sign of rising long-run inflation
MCR-071.x:
Basis: Estrella & Mishkin (1998); Harvey (1988) – the yield curve as a recession predictor.
Analysis: An inverted curve (short yields > long) reflects expected future policy cuts (as the economy weakens) and currently tight policy → in the US, 10-year–3-month inversions have preceded most recessions since 1960. Reliability varies (QE distorts long yields; the 2022–2024 inversion didn't promptly bring recession).
Distractors: B, C and D misread the meaning.

MCR-072.q: MPC 0.8; proportional income tax 25%; closed economy. What is the spending multiplier?
MCR-072.x:
Basis: Keynesian model (multiplier with proportional tax).
Working: k = 1 / [1 − MPC × (1 − t)] = 1 / (1 − 0.8 × 0.75) = 1 / (1 − 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5×.
Analysis: Proportional taxes leak each spending round → the multiplier falls from 5 (MCR-049) to 2.5. Proportional taxes are also automatic stabilisers (MCR-053). Open economies leak via imports → smaller still.

MCR-073.q: A common rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of negative quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth signal a technical recession.
MCR-073.e: True (rule of thumb). Bodies like the NBER use broader definitions.
MCR-073.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics; NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee.
Analysis: True (as a rule of thumb). Two consecutive quarters of seasonally adjusted real GDP decline quarter-on-quarter is a 'technical recession'. The NBER (US) uses a broader definition: a significant, widespread decline lasting more than a few months, across many indicators (jobs, income, output, retail sales).
Note: Vietnam mainly reports year-on-year growth – take care applying the quarter-on-quarter convention.

MCR-074.e: It argues for early policy response in deep recessions.
o: Prolonged unemployment erodes skills, raising the natural rate
MCR-074.x:
Basis: Blanchard & Summers (1986) – hysteresis in European unemployment.
Analysis: Hysteresis: long unemployment erodes skills, networks and motivation; firms avoid hiring the long-term unemployed → cyclical becomes structural unemployment → a higher natural rate and lower potential output. Implication: act early and forcefully in deep recessions to avoid permanent damage.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't hysteresis.

MCR-075.q: Select ALL possible causes of demand-pull inflation:
MCR-075.e: Rising productivity expands supply and eases price pressure.
o: Strong fiscal expansion near full employment
Large unsterilised remittance and capital inflows
A sharp rise in labour productivity
MCR-075.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (demand-pull inflation).
Analysis: Demand-pull sources: (A) runaway credit growth – more spending and investment; (B) strong fiscal expansion near full employment; (C) an export boom – higher domestic income; (D) large remittances and inflows not sterilised (MCR-088) → money growth.
Distractors: (E) Productivity gains raise supply and ease prices.
Note: Vietnam in 2007–2008 and 2010–2011 saw high inflation from credit booms combined with price shocks.

MCR-076.e: What's true for one isn't necessarily true for all (fallacy of composition).
o: If everyone saves more in a recession, demand and income fall and total saving may not rise
Government should raise taxes in recessions
MCR-076.x:
Basis: Keynes (1936) – paradox of thrift.
Analysis: In a recession, if all households save more at once → consumption and demand fall → incomes fall → total saving may not rise and can even fall. What's rational for one isn't for all – the fallacy of composition.
Distractors: B – short-run higher saving cuts demand; C – saving depends on income; D – raising taxes in recession worsens it.
Note: In the long run, high saving funds investment and growth (MCR-094) – the paradox mainly applies short-term when demand is deficient.

MCR-077.q: Over the year the nominal VND/USD rate rises 3% (VND depreciates), US inflation is 2% and Vietnam's 4%. By roughly how much does the VND real exchange rate change (% positive = real depreciation)?
MCR-077.e: %ΔRER ≈ %Δe + π* − π = 3 + 2 − 4 = 1%: a 1% real depreciation, making Vietnamese goods slightly more competitive.
MCR-077.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics (real exchange rate RER = e × P*/P).
Working: %ΔRER ≈ %Δe + π* − π = 3% + 2% − 4% = 1% → a 1% real VND depreciation.
Analysis: The VND fell 3% nominally, but Vietnam's inflation 2 points above the US offsets most of it → price competitiveness improves only 1%. A full view needs the multilateral real effective rate (REER) against trading partners.

MCR-078.q: Match each transaction with its balance of payments component (BPM6):
MCR-078.e: Correct classification helps read the central bank's BoP releases.
p: FDI profits repatriated to the parent
Foreign investors funding a new factory
MCR-078.x:
Basis: IMF Balance of Payments Manual BPM6 (2009).
Analysis: Phone exports and component imports – goods trade balance (current account). FDI profits sent to parents – primary (investment) income in the current account. Remittances – secondary income (personal transfers – MCR-079). Foreign investors funding a factory – direct investment (financial account).
Note: Vietnam typically runs a goods trade surplus but a large primary income deficit from FDI profit repatriation.

MCR-079.q: Under BPM6, workers' remittances are recorded in secondary income in the current account.
MCR-079.e: True. Personal transfers are part of secondary income.
MCR-079.x:
Basis: IMF BPM6 paras 12.21–12.23 (personal transfers).
Analysis: True. Remittances from workers abroad are personal transfers between resident and non-resident households → secondary income in the current account. Distinguish: compensation of short-term workers abroad (still residents) is primary income.
Note: Vietnam receives roughly USD 15 billion a year in remittances (per recent reports) – an important FX source supporting the currency.

MCR-080.q: The 'impossible trinity' (Mundell) says a country can't simultaneously have:
MCR-080.e: At most two of the three can be chosen.
o: A fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility and independent monetary policy
Growth, low inflation and low unemployment
A trade surplus, budget surplus and low debt
MCR-080.x:
Basis: Mundell (1963), Fleming (1962); Obstfeld & Taylor – the trilemma.
Analysis: A country can't have all three: a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility and independent monetary policy – at most two. E.g., Hong Kong (fixed + open capital, no monetary independence); the US (open capital + independence, floating); China (managed peg + independence, capital controls).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the trilemma.
Note: Vietnam runs a central rate with a band and partial capital controls – a middle path; when the Fed hikes, pressure on the VND and domestic rates rises.

MCR-081.q: Spot is VND 25,000/USD; 1-year VND rate 6%, USD 4%. Under covered interest parity, what is the 1-year forward rate (2 decimals)?
MCR-081.x:
Basis: Covered interest parity (CIP): F = S × (1 + i_domestic)/(1 + i_foreign).
Working: F = 25,000 × 1.06 / 1.04 = 25,000 × 1.019231 ≈ 25,480.77 VND/USD.
Analysis: The higher-yielding currency (VND) trades at a forward discount (≈ 1.92% a year) – otherwise riskless arbitrage would exist. Importers use forwards to lock costs; forward points reflect rate differentials, not an FX forecast.
Check: 25,480.77 × 1.04 / 1.06 ≈ 25,000 ✓.

MCR-082.q: A currency depreciation always improves the trade balance immediately.
MCR-082.e: False. Under the J-curve, the balance may worsen first as import prices rise before volumes adjust.
MCR-082.x:
Basis: J-curve effect (Magee 1973); Marshall–Lerner condition (MCR-083).
Analysis: False. Right after devaluation, contracts are at old prices and volumes haven't adjusted → import costs (in local currency) rise → the trade balance may first worsen. Over time exports rise and imports fall → the balance improves (a J shape), if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds.

MCR-083.q: The Marshall–Lerner condition for a devaluation to improve the trade balance is:
MCR-083.e: Economies assembling heavily imported inputs may gain little from devaluation.
o: The sum of (absolute) price elasticities of export and import demand exceeds 1
MCR-083.x:
Basis: Marshall (1923), Lerner (1944) – the Marshall–Lerner condition.
Analysis: Devaluation improves the trade balance if the sum of the absolute price elasticities of export and import demand exceeds 1 – volumes respond enough to outweigh the price effect. Processing economies importing many inputs for export (like Vietnam – electronics, textiles) gain little, as imported input costs rise too.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the condition.

MCR-084.q: Exports of goods and services 400; imports 380; net primary income −20; net secondary income +15 (USD billion). What is the current account balance?
MCR-084.x:
Basis: IMF BPM6 (current account components).
Working: Current account = (exports − imports of goods and services) + net primary income + net secondary income = (400 − 380) + (−20) + 15 = 20 − 20 + 15 = USD 15 billion (surplus).
Analysis: The trade surplus of 20 is cancelled by negative primary income (FDI profit outflows); remittances (+15) produce the current-account surplus – a typical Vietnamese structure.
Check: 20 − 20 + 15 = 15 ✓.

MCR-085.q: Select ALL common effects of VND depreciation against USD:
MCR-085.e: Unhedged USD borrowers suffer FX losses.
o: USD debt service in VND terms rises
MCR-085.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics.
Analysis: VND weakening against the USD: (A) exports get cheaper in USD → more competitive; (B) imported inputs cost more in VND; (C) USD debt service rises in VND – FX losses if unhedged; (D) imported inflation pressure (fuel, materials).
Distractors: (E) USD debt rises in VND terms, not falls.
Note (equity analysis): exporters earning USD (seafood, textiles, wood) gain; firms with big USD debt or imported inputs (power, steel using imported ore) lose.

MCR-086.q: A current account deficit corresponds to domestic investment exceeding national saving.
MCR-086.e: True by the identity CA = S − I.
MCR-086.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (identity CA = S − I; Y = C + I + G + NX).
Analysis: True. From the national income identity: national saving − investment = CA. Investment above national saving → borrowing/receiving foreign capital → a current-account deficit. A deficit isn't bad per se if it funds productive investment (FDI); it's risky when financed by short-term money for consumption.

MCR-087.q: National saving is 30% of GDP and investment 33%. What is the current account (% GDP)?
MCR-087.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (CA = S − I).
Working: CA = S − I = 30% − 33% = −3% of GDP.
Analysis: The 3% gap is financed by foreign capital (FDI, borrowing, portfolio). Risk depends on the financing mix (FDI is steadier than short-term money), FX reserves (MCR-090) and external debt.

MCR-088.q: The central bank buys USD to build reserves and issues bills to absorb the equivalent VND. This is:
MCR-088.e: Aim: build reserves without expanding money supply, containing inflation.
MCR-088.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics (sterilised intervention).
Analysis: The SBV buys USD → injecting VND (raising base money); it simultaneously issues bills draining the same VND → money supply unchanged → sterilised intervention. Aim: build reserves and steady the rate without inflation. Cost: interest on bills; effectiveness fades if prolonged.
Distractors: B – QE buys domestic assets to ease; C – devaluation changes the official rate; D – it isn't fiscal.

MCR-089.q: Under relative purchasing power parity in the long run, a country with higher inflation will:
MCR-089.e: PPP explains long-run trends better than short-run moves.
o: See its currency depreciate by roughly the inflation differential
MCR-089.x:
Basis: Cassel (1918) – relative purchasing power parity.
Analysis: Relative PPP: %Δe ≈ π_domestic − π_foreign → a higher-inflation country's currency depreciates by roughly the inflation gap (preserving equal purchasing power). PPP explains long-run trends better than short-run moves (driven by capital flows, rates and expectations).
Distractors: B, C and D contradict the theory.

MCR-090.q: FX reserves are often assessed in months of imports, with 3 months the traditional minimum adequacy threshold.
MCR-090.e: True (rule of thumb). The IMF also uses a composite ARA metric covering short-term debt and money supply.
MCR-090.x:
Basis: IMF – Assessing Reserve Adequacy (ARA, 2011, 2015).
Analysis: True (as a rule of thumb). Three months of imports is the traditional minimum. The IMF's composite ARA metric for emerging markets combines exports, short-term debt, other long-term liabilities and M2 (capital flight risk) – 100–150% of ARA is adequate.
Note: Vietnam's reserves have hovered around 3 months of imports recently – below ARA recommendations in some IMF assessments; check the latest data.

MCR-091.q: The most important source of long-run per-capita income growth is:
MCR-091.e: Pure capital accumulation runs into diminishing returns.
o: Productivity growth (technology, total factor productivity – TFP)
MCR-091.x:
Basis: Solow (1956, 1957); endogenous growth theory (Romer 1990).
Analysis: In the long run, per-capita income grows mainly through productivity – technological progress and total factor productivity (TFP). Capital accumulation alone faces diminishing returns → growth slows near the steady state (MCR-094).
Distractors: B, C and D affect only the short run or prices.

MCR-092.q: By the 'rule of 70', an economy growing 7% a year doubles in about how many years?
MCR-092.x:
Basis: Rule of 70 (from ln 2 ≈ 0.693).
Working: Doubling time ≈ 70 / growth rate (%) = 70 / 7 = 10 years. Exact: ln 2 / ln 1.07 = 0.6931 / 0.06766 ≈ 10.24 years.
Analysis: For investing: a portfolio compounding 15% a year doubles in about 4.7 years (70/15) – showing compounding's power (the rule of 72 gives similar results).

MCR-093.q: Growth accounting: GDP grows 6%; capital share 0.4; capital grows 8%; labour 1%. What is the TFP contribution (percentage points)?
MCR-093.x:
Basis: Solow growth accounting (1957): g_Y = g_TFP + α × g_K + (1 − α) × g_L.
Working: g_TFP = 6 − 0.4 × 8 − 0.6 × 1 = 6 − 3.2 − 0.6 = 2.2 points.
Analysis: Capital contributes 3.2 points (53%), labour 0.6 (10%), TFP 2.2 (37%). A low TFP share means capital-driven, extensive growth that is prone to diminishing returns.
Check: 2.2 + 3.2 + 0.6 = 6 ✓.

MCR-094.q: In the Solow model, a higher saving rate raises the steady-state income level but not the long-run growth rate.
MCR-094.e: True. Long-run per-capita growth is driven by technological progress.
MCR-094.x:
Basis: Solow (1956) – neoclassical growth model.
Analysis: True. A higher saving rate → higher steady-state capital per worker → a higher income level (level effect); growth is temporarily faster during transition, but at the new steady state, long-run per-capita growth is set only by technological progress (no growth-rate effect).

MCR-095.q: Select ALL factors that raise potential growth:
MCR-095.e: Money supply only affects the short run; in the long run mainly prices.
MCR-095.x:
Basis: Growth theory (Romer 1990; Acemoglu & Robinson 2012 – institutions).
Analysis: Drivers of potential growth: (A) human capital quality; (B) transport, energy and digital infrastructure (MCR-060); (C) transparent institutions, property rights, contract enforcement; (D) innovation and technology transfer (raising TFP).
Distractors: (E) Money supply works only short-term; in the long run it mainly affects prices (MCR-037, MCR-065).

MCR-096.e: Cheap-labour advantages fade; productivity drivers are needed.
o: A country reaching middle income but stalling for long, unable to reach high income because it fails to shift to productivity- and innovation-led growth
MCR-096.x:
Basis: Gill & Kharas (2007), World Bank – the 'middle-income trap'; World Bank Vietnam 2045 report.
Analysis: Countries reach middle income on cheap labour, capital accumulation and moving workers from farms to industry; as these advantages fade, failing to shift to productivity, innovation and high skills → prolonged slowdown short of high income.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the definition.
Note: Vietnam targets high-income status by 2045 – escaping the trap is the central challenge.

MCR-097.q: GDP is VND 12,000 trillion and employment 52 million. What is labour productivity (VND million per worker, 2 decimals)?
MCR-097.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (labour productivity = GDP / employed workers).
Working: VND 12,000 trillion = 12,000 × 10¹² = 1.2 × 10¹⁶; productivity = 1.2 × 10¹⁶ / 52 × 10⁶ ≈ 2.3077 × 10⁸ ≈ VND 230.77 million per worker.
Analysis: Unit control is the most error-prone step (trillion = 10¹², million = 10⁶). Low productivity versus regional peers reflects large agricultural and informal shares.
Check: 230.77 × 52 ≈ 12,000 (trillion, after conversion) ✓.

MCR-098.q: Conditional convergence says poorer countries tend to grow faster if they share similar fundamentals (saving, institutions, human capital).
MCR-098.e: True. There is no unconditional convergence across all countries.
MCR-098.x:
Basis: Barro (1991); Mankiw, Romer & Weil (1992) – conditional convergence.
Analysis: True. In the Solow model, poorer countries (low capital per worker, high marginal returns) grow faster – but only with similar fundamentals (saving, population growth, human capital, institutions) → converging to the same steady state. There's no unconditional convergence: many poor countries don't catch up due to weak institutions and human capital.

MCR-099.q: A rising ICOR over time indicates:
MCR-099.e: ICOR = investment / ΔGDP, but it's affected by the cycle and investment mix (infrastructure has lags).
o: More investment is needed per unit of extra output – lower investment efficiency
MCR-099.x:
Basis: Development economics (Harrod–Domar; ICOR = I / ΔY).
Analysis: A rising ICOR → more investment needed per unit of growth → falling investment efficiency. But ICOR is cyclical (small ΔY in recessions spikes it) and depends on investment mix (infrastructure has long lags, high short-term ICOR) → interpret carefully, using multi-year trends.
Distractors: B is the opposite; C and D aren't directly related.

MCR-100.q: Total investment is 33% of GDP and GDP growth 6.6%. What is the ICOR?
MCR-100.x:
Basis: Development economics (ICOR = (I/Y) / g).
Working: ICOR = 33% / 6.6% = 5×.
Analysis: Five units of investment are needed per extra unit of GDP. At ICOR 5, 8% growth requires investment of 40% of GDP – or a lower ICOR (more efficient investment). Vietnam's ICOR has typically ranged around 5–7 across periods.
Check: 6.6% × 5 = 33% ✓.
